items.title: Why Flying With a Bike is Always a Gamble (And How to Improve Your Odds)
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: There are no guarantees once your bike disappears on the luggage belt. But understanding TSA habits and airline loopholes gives your frame a fighting chance.
items.lbText:

I travel with a bike more than most people, and it terrifies me every single time. After having a Look 795 Blade RS arrive broken in a Scicon AeroComfort case, I went down a deep rabbit hole—talking to the TSA and picking apart the fine print of airline contracts of carriage. Since then, I’ve learned even more by talking to the people who actually design bike luggage. Despite still being absolutely terrified of landing with a broken bike, I’ve learned a lot of info that rarely gets talked about. Here’s what I know about flying with a bike right now.

When you check baggage on a flight, you are agreeing to a contract of carriage. You might occasionally have to explicitly sign a waiver, but typically, you’ll hear nothing about it. You’ve still agreed to it, and if something happens to your bike, you are bound by those terms.

This contract outlines the liability an airline accepts when taking your property. Look carefully, because some airlines exclude bike liability completely, while others cap it at a specific amount that likely won’t cover a replacement frame. That cap drops even lower on international flights. The contract will also dictate what type of case is considered acceptable, and most airlines specify a hard case.

On top of airline rules, the TSA will almost always open your bag because it’s too large to be scanned. When I spoke to Sean Harbaugh, a supervisory TSA officer with 20 years of experience, he told me their biggest request is that cyclists stop packing extra gear and clothing into the case alongside the bike.

Add all of this up, and the reality is far less black and white than the airlines want you to believe—a gray area I’ll explain in a moment. But first, if your bike gets damaged, expect a huge fight to get a payout, and it will likely be less than you need. Regardless of the amount though, if you want any chance of succeeding, you must check your bike at the airport before you leave. You cannot make a claim once you walk out those doors. Open the case, check carefully for damage, and start the claim immediately if you find a problem. During that process, explicitly request that the security video of the TSA checking your bike be preserved. The inspection is always on video, but that footage will be overwritten unless you demand they pull it.

This is pretty obvious, and it’s what everyone thinks is the issue. Baggage handlers generally do not care about your bike. Sometimes they are outright hostile with it, but typically, they just don’t care. The bag will almost always get flipped on its side, and it will sometimes get slammed on the ground, a luggage cart, or a belt. Make sure whatever case you use will protect your bike from this treatment.

If your bars come off and you can fold them down, things are pretty easy. Even a cardboard box will typically work, although my favorite option for this scenario is the Topeak PakGo X. The real challenge comes when you are dealing with a modern bike and can’t take your bars off.

If that’s what you are up against, look for something that keeps your case from being crushed from the sides. The Orucase Sentinel is an incredible option that uses a rather genius internal aluminum roll cage. It protects the controls by running a rigid expansion bar through the drops that secures into place inside the case. I have a friend who actually uses the Scicon that broke my bike, but he uses PVC pipes to create an anti-crush system very similar to what Orucase is doing. Of course, a more traditional hard case will win out if you are only looking at what it takes to protect your bike from the baggage handlers.

After I had my bike broken, I swore I’d never fly with another soft case. Then I started using the Orucase Sentinel and had a conversation with the founder of Orucase, Isaac Howe. I’ve talked to him for years about the theory of bike cases, but recently we talked about what actually constitutes a “hard case.”

In talking to him, I realized I’d made a mistake in blindly believing the airlines. It seems like what the contract of carriage means is that you need a giant plastic or aluminum vault like a Shokbox or a Bike Box Alan. The reality is that no one has ever litigated it. If you have a soft outer material that covers a rigid internal structure, you can argue that it is still a hard case. Should someone go to court with that line of reasoning, they might well win. No one will actually go to court, though, so my advice is to think carefully about what you say if you ever make a claim. Your case could well qualify as a hard case, so don’t make the mistake of calling it a soft case.

The reason all of this matters is that you aren’t just protecting your bike from baggage handlers. If you were, a traditional hard case would be the undisputed answer. Instead, Howe told me that one of the hardest things to design for is the TSA. You meticulously pack your bike, everything is safe inside a hard outer shell, and then a TSA agent opens it and doesn’t bother putting it back together correctly. You might end up with a broken bike even though the case was strong enough to withstand anything a baggage handler could throw at it.

For my most recent trip, I ended up choosing the Post Carry Co. Loomer for this exact reason. It helped that Factor CEO Calvin Chan told me he carries the Factor ONE Bugatti edition bikes all over the world in that case, but it was also just the way it works. It’s essentially a hard case, but its simple closure system and the ease of seeing the bike made me think the TSA might be less apt to mess it up.…

items.title: Two More Teams Said to Be Interested in Roglič, Including a Major Wildcard
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Decision on retirement or return due ‘soon’ for European champion Primož Roglič.
items.lbText:
Primoż Roglič at the start of Il Lombardia (Photo: Silvia Colombo/NurPhoto) (Photo: Silvia Colombo)

The Slovenian had a spectacular return to form this autumn, winning the European time trial championships and taking secondo overall in the Vuelta a España.

At the same time there has been plenty of rumblings about his future plans, with the 36 hinting he wanted to continue while also saying that Il Lombardia could be the final race of his career.

It was hard to tell if the suggestion of retirement was due to potential dissatisfaction with what he had been offered, or simply a way of raising the stakes.

Indicating he was prepared to walk away was a message to anyone dithering that time was ticking and terms must be decided.

That race was two weeks ago and since then the possibilities have, apparently, continued to grow.

The latest? Two more teams are apparently interested in the rider, including one which was probably not on anyone’s radar but, for that squad at least, could make a lot of sense.

Unibet Rose Rockets is the latest to be linked to Roglič, with team founder Bas Tietema telling Sporza at the Tour de France presentation that he would potentially be of interest.

“There are also still a number of riders on the market without a contract, but we don’t want to make hasty decisions,” he said.

Asked if there had been any contact with Roglič, he confirmed both a historical link and a more recent one.

“A long time ago, we did get in touch with Primoz through our videos,” he said.

“And when he had a bad fall at the Vuelta, we also got in touch. He was really searching for direction then.

“I think he’d be great for almost any team. But we just need to see if Roglič is realistic for us. And I think he still has to decide if he even wants to continue riding.”

The squad is certainly of more modest stature than the others linked to the European champ.

Lotto-Intermarché, Tudor, XDS Astana, and Pinarello–Q36.5 are amongst those reported to have shown interest.

More recently his former team Visma-Lease a Bike has apparently been in touch, with Wielerflits reporting this week that several sources have confirmed talks between them.

Roglič spent eight full years with the team, finally leaving in 2023. His departure came after a Vuelta a España where he was forced to hold back and to allow teammate Sepp Kuss to win. He was a frustrated third, and headed to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe seeking sole leadership.

That in turn disappeared when Florian Lipowitz finished third in the 2025 Tour, and when the team signed Remco Evenepoel.

Visma-Lease a Bike still has Jonas Vingegaard on board, meaning any decision to rejoin would see he and Roglič needing to share top billing.

However Vingegaard will likely target the Tour de France, potentially handing Roglič the number one slot in the Vuelta and, possibly, the Giro d’Italia too.

At this point in time Roglič shares the record of most Vuelta wins with four titles. Signing again with the Dutch team could see him have very strong backing for a fifth Vuelta success, an ambition that could well keep him in the sport.

Unibet Rose Rockets wouldn’t have anything like the same manpower to support such a goal. However it would eagerly offer him top billing if it helped get the nod for the Tour de France.

With perhaps just one more year left in his legs, Roglič may ultimately opt for whoever makes him the biggest offer.

Would the Rockets have the financial clout for that? The budget would certainly need to increase but, on the plus side, signing a rider as good as Roglič would boost their chances of a Tour invite.

Being passed over this year was a disappointment; having one or more big names on the roster would be the best way to sidestep that problem next year.

Financial offers aside, there is one other factor which could make all the difference.

Some riders’ families get cold feet about them spending a lot of time on the road. Jonas Vinegaard’s wife, for example, has complained about long absences from home, including at multiple training camps.

Vingegaard contemplated retirement over the issue but was able to get Visma-Lease a Bike to relax a little on its demands.

For Roglič, there seems to be a clearer understanding back home about what is needed.

“I think it’s not time to go home yet,” his wife Lora told Slovenian publication Sportal this month

“I’m not ready for this moment, especially since it is so sudden,” she said, becoming visibly emotional when discussing his possible retirement.

“I hope it’s not that… I really wish this isn’t the last time we talk about it or that I have to look back.”

Asked if she wanted to see him continue to race, she suggested he himself wanted to.

“He’s not ready to go home yet,” she said, then joked about taking up a lot of sport herself. “What are we going to do now? I can’t run marathons.

“I think he’s not ready to go home yet, but we have to respect the decision he will make.”

It sounds like she is fully committed if he decides to go on.

Finding a team which is similarly dedicated to the project is what is needed now, particularly as there are fresh indications that he too wants to keep racing.

That’s according to Spanish newspaper AS, which reports that there will ‘soon’ be news about his future, and what it terms a new destiny.

It also reports that he has ‘the desire to continue and several offers to choose from.’

With team building camps already taking place in various countries, plus the time to knuckle back down to training again fast approaching, a decision is indeed likely in the days or weeks ahead.

items.title: Moto and Mountain Bike Icon Öhlins Debuts a Lust-Worthy Gravel Fork
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The GXF30 M.1 from the Swedish suspension brand offers clean functionality and bold aesthetics to the gravel market.
items.lbText:
The legendary auto and mountain bike suspension brand Öhlins has entered the gravel suspension market with the GXF30 M.1 short-travel fork. Öhlins has been heavily involved in mountain bikes in recent years, with particular success in downhill racing, making the pivot to gravel feel like a natural progression.

Nevertheless, the brand is coming into the market well after the other big suspension brands entered the gravel market.

Despite the crowded market, Öhlins is still leaning into its standing as one of the most well-respected suspension brands with a simple yet refined gravel option that is a direct competitor to the Fox TC 32 and the RockShox Rudy. No remote lockout, no stripped-down inverted design, just 40mm of travel delivered in a clean, highly aesthetic design.

“We are not the first suspension company entering the gravel segment, but we wanted to do it with our own philosophy. For more than 50 years, Öhlins has been dedicated to off-road racing, and we firmly believe that every off-road discipline benefits from suspension. Gravel is not an exception.

“Our objective was simple: improve rider comfort, increase grip on technical terrain, and provide greater confidence and safety on every ride. These three principles guided every engineering decision throughout the development process. The result is a suspension fork that allows riders to go faster while feeling more in control.”

When it comes to gravel suspension, there seem to be two camps. On one side are forks that are essentially smaller versions of mountain bike forks. On the other side are forks that are trying to achieve gravel suspension through unique means.

Öhlins follows the former model, building a size-down version of a mountain bike fork instead of coming in with any revolutionary ideas. It doesn’t rock the boat; instead, the GXF30 M.1 is built to be a rock-solid 40mm fork that is best suited for small bump control and traction management.

It is worth noting that the GXF30 M.1 is only offered in that 40mm travel, compared to the RockShox Rudy or the Fox TC 32 which have multiple travel options. That was the travel that the brand felt met its riding objectives without changing the geometry and fit of suspension-corrected geometry. Additionally, changing the travel would require replacing the fork’s piston rod assembly, which further cemented the plan for Öhlins to restrict the travel to 40mm.

The GXF30 M.1 does, however, have a highly adjustable crown-based lockout. Beyond just a binary lock/unlock setting, the GXF30 M.1 offers more interstitial settings to control how stiff the fork is. Adjustability is a tricky point for gravel forks, historically, especially around lockout settings. With the simple design, adjustability seems to be a big priority for Öhlins.

In terms of the fork’s construction, Öhlins has opted for 30mm stanchions—the same diameter as the Rudy—and the brand’s FTX14 damper. Dampers have been an area where gravel suspension has been split. With the gravel use case, forks can get away with limited or no damper, but it still can improve the overall feel of the fork, especially at high speeds over rough terrain.

Öhlins has zeroed in on the damper construction and the unique demands of a damper on short-travel gravel forks, as an area where its expertise in a wide variety of high-end racing suspension can make a difference.

The downside of any robust suspension damper is weight. The Öhlins GXF30 M.1 is no different, with the system weighing in at a claimed 1,249 grams. That said, that weight is still around 100 grams less than the RockShox Rudy and in line with the Fox TC 32, so Öhlins has managed to minimize the weight penalty.

The Öhlins GXF30 M.1 is available now, but in a limited run of just 300 launch edition units. The limited availability is in line with the brand’s positioning of the GXF 30M.1 as a true premium gravel fork.

Accordingly, the fork is on the more expensive side at an MSRP of $995 USD and €895 EUR. Nevertheless, at that price, the classic Öhlins Racing Yellow paint scheme is standard in launch-edition forks and does give the fork a striking yet classic look.

To learn more about the ins and outs of the GXF30 M.1, visit Öhlins’ website .

items.title: Anti-Pogačar Tour? ‘We Want to Keep the Suspense,’ Says Prudhomme
items.author: ahood
items.content: Tour de France boss Prudhomme denies the 2027 route targets Pogačar, saying more TT kilometers could keep the yellow jersey fight alive.
items.lbText:
Prudhomme denied the Tour de France course is designed against Pogačar. (Photo: Getty Images)

Is the 2027 Tour de France route designed to make life hard for Tadej Pogačar ?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme .

The Tour de France created a stir Thursday with its 2027 course reveal in what’s a radical departure from the past several editions .

Instead of endless uphill kickers and non-stop climbing that seemed like a red carpet for King Pog, the 114th edition is packed with two individual time trials and features only three major mountaintop finales.

Fan reaction was quick: This is an anti-Pogačar course .

Prudhomme pushed back, but didn’t hide the fact that this year’s design is far from ideal from the Slovenian superstar.

“We’ll never design a course for just one rider. Instead, we design courses for different types of riders,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio .

“We’ve done it for puncheurs for years because it’s more exciting to watch and less dangerous than a classic sprint finish. Now, we’re adding more time trials because we want to rebalance things.”

Prudhomme and the ASO braintrust are about to find out.

Two individual time trials totaling 71 kilometers, the most in 15 years, give Remco Evenepoel and rising French star Paul Seixas a chance to counter the Slovenian’s mountain firepower.

After watching Pogačar dominate the Tour since 2024 and perhaps listening to murmurs that the Slovenian’s dominance is becoming boring, the Tour race director wanted to change things up.

With the most individual time trial kilometers since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012, Tour officials are giving Evenepoel room to put his biggest advantage to work.

Rising French star Seixas also gets terrain to challenge the established order — if he decides to race the Tour.

“We have a rider who has dominated the time trial for years, Remco Evenepoel. There’s also Paul Seixas, who is very good in this discipline,” Prudhomme said. “This could be a way to rebalance the time lost in the mountains.”

Prudhomme’s explanation, though, gets to the heart of the challenge facing anyone trying to build suspense around cycling’s most dominant rider.

From the monuments to the grand tours, Pogačar has been all but unbeatable since 2024. Only a mid-race crash that ended his season cost him a likely Vuelta a España crown.

After several Tour editions of ever-increasingly difficult courses, ASO thought it was time for a change.

The start in the UK with three stages means that there won’t be a major mountain summit until the end of the first full week.

The rise of Evenepoel against the clock and Seixas’ growing all-around abilities means, that at least in the eyes of course designers, having more TT’s now makes more sense.

In earlier editions, course designers saw how Pogačar was crushing rivals both in time trials and in the mountains. Jonas Vingegaard stopped him in his tracks for two years.

“For time trials, when the same riders gain time in the mountains and in the time trial, there’s no incentive to increase the time for the individual time trials since the result is the same,” Prudhomme said.

So in that context, Prudhommme and Co. came up with a 2027 course that’s a bit of an old-school throwback.

Sprinters see more chances, including a day-one shot at yellow, and the time trial is back in vogue.

A flat 38km test through Loire château country in the first week should suit the pure specialists. The second TT just before the Pyrénées is on a 33km loop around Toulouse that features a short but steep “wall” with about 10km to go.

On paper, that could favor Evenepoel and perhaps even Seixas, whose TT chops are improving. He finished third to an unstoppable Belgian “aero-rocket” at the Montréal time trial worlds.

“It’s a clash of styles between time trial specialists who gain time in the time trial and climbers who gain time in the mountains and lose it in the time trial,” he said.

Prudhomme called the Col du Portet the Tour’s “new Tourmalet” and said the final mountain stages in the Pyrénées will prove decisive.

“This could turn the tables 48 hours before the final arrival in Paris,” he said. “We want to keep the suspense going for as long as possible.”

But will the Tour makeover work and keep the tension in the race all the way to the final weekend?

“It’s not an anti-Pogačar strategy,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio . “Pogačar loves challenges. So, he might be the one to win both time trials.”

So much for finding a chink in the Slovenian’s armor.

items.title: Velo Podcast | We Recount the War Stories of 109 Degrees One Day and Hurricane Winds the Next
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: We headed into the desert and it turned out it's hot. We talk about crazy winds and surviving the heat just to get to the climbs. Plus, answering your questions on aero math and looking at the new Garmin Edge 1060.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

We’ve been away, and we’ve all been doing big rides. This week, we dive into the aftermath of our near-death (it certainly felt like death) ride through Death Valley. Logan Jones-Wilkins is still away, so that leaves me, Mike Levy, and Lisa Charlebois to discuss our ride together. We experienced temps of 109, some of us had heat exhaustion, and there was a hurricane that brought gale-force winds. That last one was especially interesting given I was on an aero bike with 65mm wheels.

Before we get into the details of the big ride, though, we’ve got some listener questions. You guys want to know why I never specify a number when I quote aero savings, and I have answers. We also give some bike recommendations and listen to a recounting of an awful bike accident before we jump into talking about the new Garmin Edge 1060 and what we think of the idea of voice control.

Then it’s time to recount the Death Valley trip. Why did Lisa drop us on the first major hill, and what caused her husband to find himself puking on the side of the road? Not to give anything away, but we have a poll this week about what happens if you have a massive goal—whether it’s a race or a big ride—and you don’t complete it. Listen to the show and let us know your thoughts.

items.title: Jolanda Neff Follows Kate Courtney in Latest MTB-to-Road Pivot
items.author: ahood
items.content: Neff joins Courtney in road racing transition as flexible teams and new points rules give top stars more freedom to race across disciplines.
items.lbText:
Jolanda Neff joins Fenix-Premier Tech for 2027. (Photo: Billy Ceusters/Getty Images)

Jolanda Neff joins the growing mini-trend of off-road champions taking their talent to the WorldTour road peloton.

Neff, 33, is heading back to the pavement to join Fenix-Premier Tech in 2027.

“I’m really excited to join Fenix-Premier Tech, a team that unites mountain biking, cyclocross and road racing at a world-class level,” Neff said.

The Tokyo Olympic mountain bike champion is the latest in a growing list of off-road stars exploring what their engines can do inside the road peloton.

Cycling has had a long history of cross-discipline pollination, and the latest iteration has been roadies crossing over to gravel to explore new possibilities in the booming dirt-road race scene.

At the same time, some major off-road stars are coming back to the road.

Neff’s move comes with an important distinction because she isn’t hanging up the mountain bike.

Fenix-Premier Tech offers a structure to allow her to keep her irons hot in road, cyclocross, and MTB.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot led the way for this latest MTB-to-road pivot.

The Frenchwoman returned to road racing with Visma-Lease a Bike in 2025 after stampeding to Olympic MTB gold in Paris.

She promptly won Paris-Roubaix and the Tour de France Femmes . Some comeback. Of course, the former road world champion already knew her way around a peloton.

Kate Courtney is the latest cross-over story.

The American mountain bike world champion won the 2026 U.S. road title and joined FDJ United-Suez in July, turning an experiment on skinny tires into a new career chapter in the WorldTour.

Another top move comes from Axelle Dubau-Prévot — the younger half-sister of Ferrand-Prévot — who is joining SD Worx–Protime on a two-year deal.

She broke out in gravel in 2024-25 and was picked up by EF Education-Oatly, where she raced a mixed program and hit 10th at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2026.

The men have plenty of company in the multi-lane discipline craze.

Mathieu van der Poel , Wout van Aert, and Tom Pidcock made crossing disciplines part of their superstar identities.

Of course, nothing is a guarantee even for the world’s most gifted racers. Van der Poel has won world titles in cyclocross, road, and gravel, but he is still chasing mountain biking .

Alan Hatherly joined Jayco-AlUla in 2025 and combined WorldTour racing with his mountain bike ambitions . The idea was to up his overall depth and skillset by pushing into unfamiliar territory.

“I was always interested in road racing and testing my full potential as a cyclist,” Hatherly told Velo in an earlier interview. “I want to keep learning and growing as an athlete. This was the ultimate challenge for me at this point in my career.”

Of course not. Cyclists have been switching lanes ever since people were paid to race bikes.

Taylor Phinney — who raced track and road in his pro career — recently came out of retirement to try to revive USA Cycling’s bid to field a men’s team pursuit squad in track cycling in the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games .

Cadel Evans went from winning MTB World Cups to becoming Australia’s first Tour de France winner.

Traditionally, salaries were much better on the road, but that’s not always the case, especially for the headline off-road stars.

This latest cross-over boom is also fueled by a chance to chase prestigious Olympic medals and world titles in multiple disciplines.

What’s different these days is the flexibility offered from top teams.

In the past, road teams were often reluctant to see their Tour de France stars race over roots and mud for what was perceived as a risk to road ambitions.

That’s changed and several teams are embracing multi-discipline, cross-pollination racing programs.

A recent decision by the UCI to allow points to count across disciplines in team rankings will also give teams an incentive to allow more riders to experiment and compete on any surface.

Neff’s future teammate Puck Pieterse — who won a Tour de France Femmes stage and the elite XCO world title in 2024 — is another rider switching lanes smoothly between road, gravel, cyclocross, and mountain bike.

And all with the full backing of her team.

For Neff — who twice won the Swiss national road title and hit top 10s in world championships and Olympic road racing earlier in her career — the move is her latest challenge.

“I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider in every aspect, as well as sharing all my experience with other riders,” Neff said. “I have always admired how this team puts a strong focus on women and on creating professional structures for them, as well as developing young riders with a long-term vision.”

Gravel remains the favored escape route for roadies right now.

But for ambitious off-road champions, the road is looking just as good coming the other way.

items.title: The Tour de France Just Made the Anti-Pogačar Route for 2027
items.author: ahood
items.content: Or about as anti-Pog as you can get, that is. Can 71km of time trials and fewer summit finishes help Evenepoel challenge for the 2027 Tour? Here's why it still won't matter to Pogačar.
items.lbText:
Want to make Tadej Pogačar work for a record sixth Tour de France ?

Give Remco Evenepoel 71 kilometers against the clock, trim the summit finishes down to three, and deliver an old-school course without any gravel gimmicks or double assaults of Alpe d’Huez.

Perhaps that’s what ASO was thinking when the 2027 Tour de France route was unveiled Thursday in Paris with a course that some think could unsettle the world’s best cyclist.

Whether Evenepoel or anyone else can actually pull it off is another matter.

Two individual time trials in 2027 provide the most kilometers against the clock since 2012 when Bradley Wiggins won.

And with just three official summit finishes on the route, that’s fewer obvious opportunities for Pogačar to unload on his rivals.

And that presents an interesting question: Is this an anti-Pogačar Tour?

Tour officials deny they design a course in favor or against one rider’s abilities, and that also assumes anyone could design a course the Slovenian cannot conquer.

But will this Tour course give Evenepoel and others a fighting chance?

Evenepoel loves to time trial and this Tour is loaded with them.

The first is 38km from Blois to Chambord on stage 7 on a pure specialists course, followed by another 33km around Toulouse on stage 16 featuring a short ramp with 10km to go.

On paper, that should give Evenepoel — arguably the best time trialist of this generation — a huge advantage.

Both are strategically placed just before the decisive climbing blocks in the Alps and Pyrénées.

It’s the most TT miles in a Tour since Wiggins and the 2012 edition, when a prologue and two long TTs totaling just over 100km helped him win the UK’s first yellow jersey.

But how much time could Evenepoel actually take from Pogačar, who will be coming off his horrific crash at the Vuelta a España ?

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. One second per kilometer across 71km produces a cushion of 1:11. Double that and Evenepoel banks 2:22.

That’s also assuming a lot. Pogačar is no slouch against the clock, and usually gives away only a few fistfuls of seconds to Evenepoel.

Last year, he lost about 1 second per kilometer to Evenepoel in 26km late in the race when he already had yellow on ice. In 2025, when the TT came in the first week, Pogi only lost 16 seconds on 33km to Evenepoel.

But the layout for 2027 could set up an intriguing yo-yoing GC race if Pogi slightly bends the knee in the time trials.

A minute’s disadvantage would give Pogačar something to chase going into the Alps. Assuming Evenepoel can stay close, he might even be able to claw back more time and perhaps even reclaim yellow ahead of the Pyrénées.

That’s the highlight reel playing for everyone inside the Paris offices at ASO.

The bigger upside for the Belgian “aero-rocket” could come against everyone else.

Jonas Vingegaard can hold his own against the clock, but 71km gives Evenepoel a chance to build a buffer against the Dane and all the other podium contenders.

For other climbers dreaming of moving up the GC, these TT kilometers could torpedo their yellow jersey ambitions before the first week is out.

Or this Remco TT tailgate party might simply light Pogačar’s fuse to attack even more.

There’s been some grumbling that Pogačar’s relentless domination is getting boring.

Perhaps to counter that, the Tour braintrust delivered a relatively “old-school” Tour route.

There’s no first-week cobblestone stage or a hipster gravel route across the Vosges for Pogačar to smash everyone in the first week.

Even with the UK start, this is cookie-cutter stuff, with sprints and the first time trial stacked up before the Alps.

Some look to a relative dearth of summit finales with only three as evidence of another Anti-Pog bias.

It’s true that with only three true mountaintop finales, there are fewer favorable opportunities for Pogačar to crush souls. But make no mistake, Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and the Col du Portet are the real deal. It will be a huge ask for Evenepoel or anyone else to even stay close to Pogačar once he’s off the leash.

But this Tour route is harder than it looks on paper. The entire Tour route still stings with 53,450 meters of total climbing, and there are three more brutal mountain stages across the Alps, the Massif Central, and Pyrénées.

Sallanches packs 3,750 meters of climbing in a dress rehearsal for worlds. Mende stings at the end of a march across the Massif Central. And the penultimate mountain stage into Laruns delivers another 4,300 meters.

Those are massive Pogačar opportunities to make up for any lost ground.

Christian Prudhomme and company might be in for a rude surprise if they’re hoping their course will somehow muzzle Pogačar.

One can already imagine the Slovenian and UAE brass going over the race details.

Pogačar is known to attack at any point, so who’s to say he might not try to drive a split in the first week if the wind kicks up in Brittany?

It’s the other non-summit finales that could prove most pro-Pog.

Stage 10 is a dress rehearsal for the road worlds, with double-passage up and down the Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%) with 3750m of climbing with a downhill blinder to the line.

The final mountain stage to Laruns sends the race over Burdincurutcheta, Bagargui, Soudet, and Marie Blanque before the descent to the finish.

And there’s still the decisions to come on who’s racing where. Pogačar, Vingegaard, and Evenepoel all seem destined on a Tour rematch.

But perhaps more than Evenepoel, this route could favor Paul Seixas.

He can time trial as well as Pogačar and has the potential to climb even better than Evenepoel in the six mountain stages.

There are whispers that Seixas might opt to race the Giro d’Italia next year in a chance to win a grand tour, but this Tour route might tempt him back.

More than Evenepoel, this route could be ideal for Seixas to go even further than he did with fourth in his 2026 debut and perhaps even take it to Pogačar.…

items.title: The Best Gifts for Biking Families
items.author: Emily LaPointe
items.content: Give 'em more two-wheel fun with these eight products
items.lbText:
If there’s one thing most adventure-loving families can agree on, it’s this: bikes do it all, from thrill rides to zipping over to a friend’s house to the school or work commute. Luckily, there’s never been a better time to raise a biker, thanks to the wide range of children’s cycling gear out there. These eight products from REI make awesome holiday gifts for aspiring shredders, from bikes to packs to safety equipment. The only catch? Better be prepared to get on your own bike and chase these well-outfitted kids around.

For young kids learning to ride, the key is having the right bike at the right time, so they can build skills and confidence. Built for young riders ages 3 to 5, the REV 14 from REI Co-op is the perfect intermediate step between a balance bike and a real-deal frame. The design allows for balance bike-style riding, but the REV pedals are fully functional (it’s also training-wheel compatible). Front and rear handbrakes teach speed control, an easily adjustable seat accommodates fast-growing kids, and the sturdy aluminum frame is hand-me-down durable.

The best kids’ gear fits and performs just as well as the adult equivalent, and that’s exactly what the Moki 3 does. It’s sized for children (ages 4 to 12), but its design, materials, comfort, and functionality are adult level. The Moki 3 includes breathable mesh shoulder straps and a light foam backpanel, as well as a 1.5-liter hydration reservoir. The Moki’s spacious main compartment and zippered front pocket can hold everything your little one needs, from layers to snacks to their favorite toy.

Here’s a great parent problem to have: You need to train to keep up with your burgeoning speed demon. If that’s a reality for someone on your list, this bike trainer is the answer. The KICKR Core 2 is compatible with most 8- to 13-speed bikes, and its highly customizable design means users can dial in the right amount of resistance and build a super-effective workout. With an intuitive interface and integrated WiFi, the KICKR simplifies getting stronger when outdoor riding isn’t on the day’s agenda.

Once the training wheels come off, the most exciting gift a kid can receive is a “big kid” bike of their very own. The REV 20 from REI Co-op is the perfect upgrade, thanks to components that are designed specifically for riders ages 6 to 9, as well as smart features. Those include a freewheel wheel that lets kids get accustomed to backpedaling and front and rear handbrakes. The REV 20 also includes a sticker pack, reinforcing rule number one: Bikes are fun!

Actually, there’s another rule number one in biking: safety. Giro packs a ton of tech into this child-size helmet, kitting it out with a Mips liner (which reduces rotational forces), EPS foam covered by a hard polycarbonate shell, and 13 vents that provide airflow when your little one is putting the pedal to the metal. The Roc Loc® Jr. adjustment system makes finding the right fit simple. Protection is top notch, but what kids will love is the Scamp’s snazzy colors, which will have adults coveting this lid themselves.

For the youngest riders, a balance bike is the way to get started, and this one will get any tyke zooming around in no time. A self-stabilizing wobble effect keeps everything upright, and the toddler-size design fits little arms and legs (the recommended age is 9 to 36 months). With cute colors and an included plushy toy friend who can tag along on adventures, the WOW points the way toward a bright biking future.

It’s hard to disguise a bike with wrapping paper, but that won’t matter when your kid unboxes this well-built bike for riders ages 4 to 6. Everything from its handlebar grips to its mini V-brakes to its aluminum frame is constructed to make for a simple, confident learning experience. The GO 3’s 16-inch aluminum wheels are also outfitted with chunky tires, so some light off-roading might be on the menu once your aspiring ripper gains skills and confidence.

Take Smith’s classic mountain bike helmet design, make it child-friendly while retaining all its safety and design features, and you have the Sidekick Jr. A Mips system reduces rotational forces caused by angled impacts and 12 vents provide plenty of airflow for riding hard on hot days. The dial system is made for kid-size fingers so they can easily adjust fit for comfort. With an integrated visor and liner and two sizes, this is a full-featured helmet for kids who love to ride.

REI is a specialty outdoor retailer, headquartered near Seattle. The nation’s largest consumer co-op, REI is a growing community of 26 million members who expect and love the best quality gear and outstanding customer service. REI is a purpose-driven and values-led company dedicated to enabling life outside for all.

items.title: Coros Dura 2 Solar Review: The Infinite-Battery Garmin Alternative (And the Detail Everyone Will Miss)
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The 120-hour battery life and ultra-thin design steal the spotlight. But the real reason to consider this head unit has nothing to do with how long it lasts.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Unique look Lighter than other comparable computers Excellent backend training infrastructure Fast rerouting and general operation Ability to schedule ride tracking Exceptionally long battery life Fantastic music player integration Uses a standard Garmin style mount 2-1 Solar gain (two hours of battery life for every hour of ride time) The best Strava live segments implementation

Lacks third party integrations Ecosystem is a walled garden Screen brightness and resolution lacking

Most people knew the original Coros Dura because it was cheap and had an incredible battery life. Today, the Coros Dura 2 launches and it’s not cheap anymore, but it brings a lot to the table. Among those things is a form factor that is unlike anything else on the market.

Of course, part of me wants to say that form factor doesn’t matter, but come on, let’s be real here—this is pretty cool. The new Coros Dura 2 Solar has a carbon fiber backplate and an anodized aluminum bezel making up what sort of looks like two pieces that stack together. The leading edge is only 5.7mm thick and looks more like a concept bike computer than real life.

It is real, though, and it works because it stacks on top of a rear section that houses a pair of buttons, the USB-C charging port, a speaker, and the solar panel. That solar panel has its own set of pressure-sensitive buttons, meaning they respond to actual physical force rather than just the light electrical touch of your finger like a smartphone screen. You’ll also find the Garmin-compatible quarter-turn mount housed in the rear section, and when you put it all together, it’s genuinely unique and very cool to look at.

The new computer isn’t just a pretty face, though. Coros has been mounting a genuine challenge to Garmin for the last few years, and this latest computer is yet another part of that narrative while also bringing unique features to market. To test it all out, I took off my Garmin watch, strapped on a Coros Pace 4 Pro, put the Garmin Edge 1050 in a drawer, and mounted the Coros Dura 2 Solar on my bars. Here’s what I found out.

There are several pillars I want to discuss regarding the Coros Dura 2 Solar, but the battery life is so far beyond what anyone else is offering that it has to be addressed first. It almost minimizes how much Coros outpaces the competition to merely list battery life as “a feature I like” in our standard Velo review format.

Currently, the longest battery life for a direct competitor is the Garmin Edge 1060, which carries a 20-hour rating for regular use and 60 hours in battery-saver mode. You could also point to the Garmin 1040 Solar and its 180-hour rating, but that comes with heavy caveats. First, it is two generations old, despite still being available. Second, that 180-hour figure requires solar charging and zero paired sensors; use it like a normal computer, and it drops to 45 hours. Both are decent numbers given the next closest option is the Wahoo Elemnt Ace with a claim of up to 30 hours.

Then there’s Coros. The Coros Dura 2 Solar isn’t just knocking it out of the park; this computer is playing a completely different sport. The baseline rating is 120 hours if you drop the GPS to single-band, or 70 hours in the more accurate dual-frequency mode. More importantly, those numbers are calculated without solar charging.

Coros claims—and I have no reason to doubt it—that the solar panel will generate two hours of ride time for every hour spent in direct sun. That means if you operate this like a normal bike computer in 2026, fully connected to sensors and actively navigating, you may never actually have to plug it in. After six hours of riding, all with the backlight turned to 100%, and multiple days sitting indoors—Coros designed the unit to stay in standby rather than powering down completely—my review unit was sitting at 93%. I stopped checking the battery percentage after that.

Focusing exclusively on the battery life does sell the Dura 2 slightly short, however. When the original Dura launched, it felt half-finished and was not a great product. Velo actually published a second first-impressions article when later firmware updates finally made it a reasonable option, but it still lagged behind the competition.

With the launch of the Dura 2, Coros is shedding that legacy. Every manufacturer has advantages and disadvantages, but if you want a reliable head unit in 2026, the Coros Dura 2 is firmly in the “yes, this is a good computer” category. A significant part of that success comes down to the ecosystem.

Because I like to self-coach, performance tracking and recovery metrics are important to me. Garmin has been the king of that space for years with Garmin Connect. However, Garmin operates a walled garden, and the hardware buy-in is expensive. Coros clearly recognized this market opportunity. The Coros Training Hub is every bit as good, and while it is also a walled garden—albeit one that allows Wahoo head units inside—the hardware is significantly cheaper. I am a big fan of the simple recovery status, as well as the implementation of metrics that mirror Joe Friel’s gold-standard CTL, ATL, and TSB models in TrainingPeaks.

A bike computer is just one piece of an overall training ecosystem but this is a solid one. I prefer a single upfront hardware purchase rather than paying recurring subscription fees for training software over time. Coros nails that, and the Dura 2 is a key piece of the puzzle.…

items.title: Tour de France 2027 Route Reveal: Brutal Mountains, Big Time Trials, and a Wide-Open Fight for Yellow
items.author: ahood
items.content: Tour de France 2027 packs 71km of time trials, three summit finishes, and a brutal Pyrénées showdown in deceptively challenging course.
items.lbText:
Pogačar will like what he sees in the 2027 Tour de France route. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France is going big on time trials and short on summit finales with its historic return to Great Britain.

Race director Christian Prudhomme unveiled the 114th edition Thursday in Paris, confirming a 3,479km route from Edinburgh to the Champs-Élysées from July 2-25.

The numbers tell the story: 21 stages, 53,450 meters of climbing, six mountain stages but only three summit finales, and two individual time trials totaling 71km, the most since 2012.

Can Remco Evenepoel dare to dream of yellow? Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard still might have the last word in this deceptively challenging course.

The race opens with three stages across Scotland, England, and Wales before returning to France via Normandy.

Then things get serious. The first week closes with the first of two time trials before driving into the Alps.

Three summit finishes await at Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and the monstrous Col du Portet in the Pyrénées in the final week.

That’s low by modern standards but these all pack an over-sized bite. There are three other mountain stages that don’t end at a summit but are still loaded with race-breaking climbs.

The Alps also include two ascents of the Côte de Domancy, a preview of the 2027 world championships course in a stage that could explode the GC.

The decisive final week packs in another time trial before the Pyrénées, a brutal Tourmalet and Col du Portet double, and a final mountain showdown to Laruns.

And the favorites? It’s shaping up to be a blockbuster.

Pogačar and Vingegaard will be looking to return to their best after injury setbacks, while rising stars Isaac del Toro and Paul Seixas could elbow in if they race.

The generous time trial distance — the most since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012 — should give Evenepoel favorable terrain, but he will still have to survive the mountain onslaught.

The Tour wraps up July 25 with loops over the dramatic Montmartre climb — yes, it’s back with three passages — before the traditional Champs-Élysées finale.

What’s missing? Iconic climbs like Alpe d’Huez or Mont Ventoux and the race barely touches the Massif Central.

Sprinters will see plenty of chances, with perhaps up to seven sprints, including the penultimate stage that gives the fast men a reason to suffer over the Pyrénées.

With 71km against the clock and a string of monster climbs, the 2027 Tour looks set to reward the complete rider.

Total distance : 3,479km Total elevation gain : 53,450 meters Total stages : 21 Flat stages : 7 Hilly stages : 6 Mountain stages : 6 Individual time trials : 2, totaling 71km, the most since 2012 Summit finishes : 3, at Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and Saint-Lary-Soulan Col du Portet

items.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 Route Reveal: Savage Puy de Dôme Finale to Decide Everything
items.author: ahood
items.content: Yorkshire hills, a historic London TTT, and a volcanic showdown. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes saves its hardest for last.
items.lbText:
Vollering, shown here celebrating last year, is the early favorite for the 2027 Tour de France Femmes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France Femmes will break new ground with its first team time trial, a wild opening weekend in Great Britain, and a spectacular final showdown atop the legendary Puy de Dôme.

Race director Marion Rousse unveiled a demanding nine-stage route Thursday in Paris that promises a tight the yellow jersey battle all the way to the final climb.

The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour starts July 30 in Leeds, England, and finishes August 7 atop the iconic volcano in the heart of central France.

In between, the peloton faces a punishing mix of Yorkshire hills, a historic team time trial through London, opportunities for sprinters and breakaways across northern France, and three decisive stages in the Massif Central.

In total, it’s 1,156km with 17,665m of climbing.

The route saves its biggest fireworks for last, with the Puy de Dôme set to crown the 2027 champion in a spectacular summit showdown.

As already confirmed the 2027 Tour de France Femmes opens with three stages in Great Britain, the race’s third foreign Grand Départ since its revival in 2022, following the Netherlands in 2024 and Switzerland in 2026.

The opening stage takes the peloton from Leeds to Manchester across 85.7km of rolling terrain.

Stage 2 could see an early GC shakeout, with a punishing 154.4km route from Manchester to Sheffield featuring seven categorized climbs and nearly 3,000m of climbing.

The peloton will face a team time trial for the first time since the Femmes revival in 2022.

The 18km course through London on August 1 finishes on The Mall.

After crossing the channel, racing resumes with three transition stages that give something for the sprinters and breakaways as the race hits French tarmac in northern France.

Stage 4 finishes in Calais and stage 5 in Magnanville, with both routes featuring difficult finales that could favor opportunists and puncheurs over the pure sprinters.

The fast finishers should get their best opportunity on stage 6 into Bourges, before the race turns into the gnarled roads of the Massif Central.

Stage 7 finishes atop La Loge des Gardes, the first major summit finale to open a wild final weekend.

The following day, six categorized climbs loom on the road to Clermont-Ferrand across the Massif Central.

The Puy de Dôme, one of the Tour de France’s most storied climbs, will be the battleground for the decisive final stage on August 7.

The twisting volcanic ascent returned to the men’s Tour in 2023 after a 35-year absence, with Michael Woods taking the win.

Now the women’s peloton will race up the legendary steeps overlooking Clermont-Ferrand.

Race organizers hope the battle for yellow to remain undecided until the final kilometer. The brutal slopes of the Puy de Dôme — 14.2km at 7.6% — could produce a dramatic, final-day reversal.

Who’s the course favor? On paper, defending champion Demi Vollering, as she targets a historic third Tour de France Femmes crown.

The Dutch star, who also won the 2026 world road title, can do it all on the punchy terrain and steep climbs of the Massif Central.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who joins Lidl-Trek for 2027, will be among her principal rivals, along with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot and Marlen Reusser.

Emerging star Paula Blasi, who joins Movistar, could also be a major contender after her fifth-place debut in 2026.

What’s missing? The course avoids both the Alps and the Pyrénées and the longer, sustained climbs that favor the pure climbers like Ferrand-Prévot and Niewiadoma.

items.title: I Tried Bikepacking with a 17-Foot Canoe and a Velduro Phantom
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: I went bikepacking and canoepacking all in one with the Velduro Phantom e-gravel bike. Not everything went to plan.
items.lbText:
Practically since the invention of the first bicycle, people have taken them on adventures. Today, we know this kind of riding by a couple of different names. There’s touring and bikepacking—and then there’s this secret third option known, as far as we can tell, only to a couple of brave adventurers in northern Washington.

Follow along as Logan Patrick Nelson and Andrew Ford set out for a cycling adventure like no other. The goal is to bring a canoe to a “weird, funky lake” about 40 miles outside Bellingham, Washington, using only bicycles, then transfer all the bikes and gear into the canoe and paddle back down a river to the ocean. They’re going start-to-finish carrying all their gear with them, no doubling back in cars to retrieve anything.

Now there’s only a few problems. Logan and Andy have never done this before: canoe-bikepacking, bike-canoepacking, or whatever you want to call it. In fact, it’s likely very few people have ever done this before, judging by the stares they get throughout the whole three-day trip.

The next problem: they have no way of bringing a canoe with them, so they have to devise their own trailer. That’s an adventure in and of itself, sending Logan all around the city looking for anything that will help him fabricate a solution to this niche problem. It’s part repurposed salvaged gear, part new fabrication, 100% DIY innovation.

Helping them make the dream of towing a 17-foot canoe up gravel climbs for this unconventional adventure is a Velduro Phantom e-gravel bike . With a 250-watt Avinox motor delivering 120Nm of torque, it’s up to the challenge of towing a loaded-down canoe. We can’t say for sure that Velduro had this use case in mind when drawing up the Phantom, but we can report that it’s squarely in the bike’s wheelhouse.

Our adventurers also make use of Aeroe bikepacking bags and mounts to bring all their gear along for the ride. Their waterproof dry bags are extra useful when the adventure turns amphibious and rapids threaten to capsize the canoe.

How does it all go? You’ll have to hit the play button to find out.
