items.title: Cannondale Closing Connecticut Office and Relocating to California; Over 100 Jobs Impacted
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Operations will be consolidated with Santa Cruz and Cervélo, two brands owned by Pon.Bike.
items.lbText:
Cannondale is closing up operations in its home state of Connecticut after over 50 years there and moving to California, the brand announced to employees and dealers today.

The move to Santa Cruz, California will bring Cannondale sales and operations closer to other brands owned by its Dutch parent company, PON.Bike. Both Santa Cruz and Cervélo operate in California.

Going forward, outside sales reps will act as a single point of contact for all three brands.

“The aim is to make it easier for retailers to work with Cannondale and access more of the Pon.Bike portfolio,” the company said in a media statement . “Each brand will retain its own identity, models and relationship with riders.”

Cannondale’s global headquarters will move to Woudenberg, Netherlands, which is Cannondale’s existing European headquarters. Global R&D and engineering will continue to be based in Freiburg, Germany.

The relocation will impact a significant number of jobs at Cannondale. Velo’s sister publication Bicycle Retailer and Industry News reports that a letter the brand filed with the Connecticut Department of Labor on Wednesday lists 143 workers who may be impacted by the closure.

“The entire office will be closed and almost all employees there will be impacted,” reads a letter to the department signed by Maggie Lansdale, global vice president of People for Cycling Sports Group, Cannondale’s business unit within Pon.

The closure will occur over the next six months and will be final in mid-2027, with some employees staying on through 2027.

Cannondale has operated in Connecticut for its entire history since its founding in 1971. The brand was acquired by Pon.Bike in 2022 after the brand bought Dorel Sports and all its brands, including Schwinn.

You can read more in Bicycle Retailer and Industry News .

items.title: Movistar Signs Spanish Star Paula Blasi in Blockbuster €1.8 Million Deal
items.author: ahood
items.content: MARCA reports that Blasi will earn 600,000 euros per season in three-year deal with Movistar, making her one of women's cycling's highest-paid riders.
items.lbText:
Pauli Blasi will race the next three seasons with Movistar. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Paula Blasi is off to Movistar on a blockbuster three-year deal to give the Spanish squad a homegrown contender to challenge the biggest names in women’s racing.

Movistar confirmed Wednesday that the 23-year-old will join from UAE Team L’IMAD in 2027 on a contract through 2029, ending months of speculation over one of the season’s most coveted signatures .

And the Spanish team is opening its wallet to make it happen.

According to MARCA , Movistar agreed to pay €85,000 to release Blasi from her UAE contract, which ran through 2027, and will pay her about €600,000 per season.

That puts its reported salary commitment above €1.8 million across three years and instantly making her one of women’s cycling’s highest-paid riders.

Movistar has not disclosed the financial terms, but Blasi’s arrival puts the Spanish team right in the middle of the race for the yellow jersey at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift .

“I’m at a point in my sporting career where I needed to take a different step and look for a team that believed in me, supported my goals and was as ambitious as I am,” Blasi said in Movistar’s official announcement.

Blasi enjoyed a breakout 2026 in only her second professional season.

She won Amstel Gold Race and then rode away with the La Vuelta Femenina to make her one of the most-prized signatures on the transfer market.

Despite some tension , she rode to fifth in her Tour de France Femmes debut while helping UAE teammate Elisa Longo Borghini reach the podium.

Now she joins Marlen Reusser and Liane Lippert in a Movistar lineup with several ways to attack the biggest races.

For Blasi, the attraction extends beyond the paycheck.

MARCA reported that UAE offered more money to retain her, but she chose Movistar after negotiations involving her agent Alex Carera , who also represents Tadej Pogačar, and team manager Sebastián Unzué.

“I’ll be able to grow, share leadership responsibilities and learn from Marlen, which will be important for my development as an athlete,” Blasi said. “And on top of that, it’s my home team. It makes me even prouder to wear the jersey.”

With Blasi, Movistar now packs a rider who could shape its women’s team for years .

Since Annemiek van Vleuten retired in 2023, the squad has worked to build another squad capable of winning across the grand tours and classics.

Blasi brings both the climbing legs and the attacking instinct to give Movistar options against rivals like Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma at the season’s biggest races .

“We are incredibly happy to finally announce Paula’s arrival on our team for the next three seasons,” Unzué said.

“Her contract represents a new step forward in terms of quality, allowing us to compete in the most important races on the calendar. I want to thank Paula for her trust and her belief in this project. We can’t wait to get started together.”

Blasi burst onto the scene in 2026 . Now for the next three years, she will be racing on the Spanish WorldTour team, and chase cycling’s biggest prizes.

And after Enric Mas won its first men’s grand tour since 2019 at La Vuelta a España, the Movistar “blues” are back.

items.title: Goodbye, Quick-Step: 24 Years of Cobbles, Glory, and Swagger
items.author: ahood
items.content: Quick-Step’s historic run as title sponsor ends. From Boonen’s cobbles to Remco’s Vuelta, here are the moments that built a cycling powerhouse.
items.lbText:
Boonen was the face of much of the Quick-Step classics heyday. (Photo: Equipe Ploeg /(c)Tim De Waele/Getty Images)

Quick-Step will close a 24-season run as title sponsor that helped turn a Belgian flooring brand into something synonymous with winning bike races.

Before today’s “superteam” era, Quick-Step was the powerhouse that drove the elite men’s peloton.

OK, other teams were obsessing on the Tour de France , but Quick-Step was the team for everything else.

For Belgians, it was their New York Yankees.

Museeuw, Boonen , Gilbert, Evenepoel — it was the team where all the big Belgian stars ended up. And few other superstars along the way as well.

Quick-Step remains a partner through 2030, but one of cycling’s longest title name partnerships is ending.

Starting in 2003, Patrick Lefevere built the squad into the “Wolfpack,” a winning machine that won across multiple terrain. Sprints, escapes, stage wins were all part of the team ethos.

But it was the classics that were essential to the team’s DNA.

The Quick-Step relationship began with Mapei in 1999, then Lefevere launched Quick-Step-Davitamon in 2003. Tom Boonen became a Belgian superstar and carried team colors for a decade.

By the 2020s, Quick-Step — a multinational flooring company — was struggling to keep pace with deep-pocketed superteams that now dominate the men’s peloton.

Czech billionaire Zdeněk Bakala remains behind the scenes, and Jurgen Foré took over as general manager after Lefevere retired.

Safety Jogger takes Quick-Step’s place alongside Soudal on the team kit in 2027. And with longtime bike sponsor Specialized also leaving, it’s an end of an era .

Even with Remco Evenepoel gone, the team is still finding ways to win. Tim Merlier and Paul Magnier now carry its winning legacy.

Here are nine chapters that explain why Quick-Step’s place in cycling history will be hard to replace.

Quick-Step’s roots run through Mapei. The powerhouse of the 1990s won world titles and sprints, and its classics roster ran so deep that Lefevere could call in the winning order at Paris-Roubaix.

By 2003, Mapei was gone, and Lefevere built Quick-Step-Davitamon with riders and staff from Mapei and Domo-Farm Frites.

The Belgian super-squad immediately delivered, with Museeuw winning Het Volk and Bettini taking Milan-San Remo in its debut season.

Only Lotto — which started in 1985 — and Cofidis and FDJ — both in 1997 — have sponsored an elite men’s pro team longer.

Quick-Step soon were the bulldogs of the spring classics. The team expected to win and became so good that even podiums were viewed as disappointments.

Bettini gave the team a champion who could win beyond the pavé . Racing for Italy, he took Olympic road gold in Athens in 2004, then consecutive world titles in 2006 and 2007.

Lefevere squeezed the value out of those victories, and Bettini emerged as the Italian swashbuckler who helped define the team’s early years.

Back in trade-team colors, the Cricket won consecutive editions of Lombardia in 2005 and 2006.

It’s hard to describe how big Tom Boonen was at the peak of his powers.

Boonen came along as Museeuw was fading and Belgian fans were hungry for a young, brash winner. They found one in Boonen, who soon became “Tomeke.”

After Lefevere stole him from Johan Bruyneel and U.S. Postal Service, Boonen lifted the team to new heights.

His career took off with huge wins at the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix in 2005. The world title in Madrid that fall made Boonen the perfect star for a new century of bike racing.

Boonen brought some football swagger to cycling, along with some off-the-bike drama, and his rivalry with Fabian Cancellara on the cobbles dominated the classics. His every move was front-page news in Belgium.

Quick-Step had its defining rider, and Belgium had its new two-wheeled idol. Lefevere loved it.

Lefevere never had the rider to chase yellow, but he built one of cycling’s best cobblestone teams.

At its peak, the crew was more than just Boonen. Stijn Devolder won Flanders in both 2008 and 2009, and Niki Terpstra was showing signs of future success.

Then came Boonen’s extraordinary 2012 season, with victories at E3 Harelbeke, Gent-Wevelgem, Flanders, and Roubaix. His long solo into the Roubaix velodrome sealed a record-tying fourth victory and the finest classics campaign of his career.

His chance to make Roubaix history with a fifth cobble was stymied by Mat Hayman in 2016, the last of his epic cobblestone dramas.

Boonen’s retirement in 2017 could have left a hole no signing could fill.

Philippe Gilbert helped people get over it. His audacious solo victory at the 2017 Tour of Flanders and hard-earned 2019 Paris-Roubaix triumph extended the team’s northern reign. Terpstra added the 2018 Flanders title between them.

Dubbed the “Wolfpack,” this was Lefevere’s dream machine, capable of winning multiple monuments with a fleet of classics crushers.

Quick-Step leaves with the team’s impressive monument legacy with 24 monuments from 2003 to 2026. They won them all during that run multiple times.

Alaphilippe won Strade Bianche, Milan-San Remo, and La Flèche Wallonne in 2019 before turning the Tour upside down.

No one ever thought Alaphilippe could win the Tour until that magical 2019 edition. Two stage victories, 14 days in yellow, and fifth overall made him the race’s great disruptors.

Lefevere never got a Tour winner, but Alaphilippe made everyone believe, at least going deep into week 3.

Consecutive world road titles in 2020 and 2021 confirmed that Alaphilippe was more than some d’Artagnan on wheels.

Lefevere had an eye for talent and wasn’t afraid to take chances on people. Gilbert was the perfect example.

Some thought his best days were behind him, but with Lefevere, Gilbert won a pair of dream races.

The same thing happened with Mark Cavendish. The slowing Manxman was still hanging around, but Lefevere offered a lifeline when his career appeared close to over.…

items.title: Garmin Brings Voice Control to Your Handlebars with the New Edge 1060
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Garmin just overhauled its cycling lineup with three major releases: the microphone-equipped Edge 1060, the touch-friendly Explore 3 series, and a new indoor smart trainer that brings built-in motion to a more accessible price point.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Garmin just dropped a three-pronged update to the brand’s cycling portfolio with new options for both the front of your bike and your winter riding. The launch includes the new flagship bike computer, the Garmin Edge 1060, along with the Edge Explore 3 and Edge Explore 3 Plus that offer recreational cyclists and e-bike riders a more affordable option. The announcement also covers a new and more affordable indoor trainer called the Tacx Nēra, which offers similar movement as the Garmin Tacx Neo 3M for half the price. Here’s what each announcement brings to the table and why you might want to care, or not, about the latest Garmin news.

Two years ago, the Garmin Edge 1050 launched, and it marked a drastic right turn for the Garmin Edge series strategy. While the previous x40 generation (540/840/1040) had solar options and incredible battery life, they also had slower processors and dimmer screens. Clearly, some market analysis had taken place at Garmin because the Edge 1050 launched with half the battery life of the previous flagship Edge 1040 Solar, but also brought one of the best screens on the market with it. Suddenly you had a lot less battery life, but the form factor was sleek and the screen was both bright and noticeably higher resolution. Some people, myself included, initially mourned the loss, but most people seemed to appreciate how gorgeous the screen actually was, and 20 hours (on the flagship 1050) really is pretty good. There’s also a battery saver mode that pushes it to 60 hours when you absolutely must have the battery life.

Now the Edge 1060 is hitting the market at $799.99, and it looks a lot more like an Edge 1050 Plus than a truly new generation. The new computer refines what works and adds new features that feel like natural extensions of the strategy that Garmin is currently executing. The headline of those features is surely the microphone.

Voice control was what you were hoping for, right? The new Garmin Edge 1060 adds a built-in microphone powering Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and allowing for “Okay, Garmin” functionality. Like a smartphone, you can keep your hands on the bar and talking to your computer lets you request ride data, pull up new routes, or report road hazards. The microphone also integrates directly with the Garmin Messenger app, allowing you to send voice messages hands-free.

The other major update to the Edge 1060 is the packaging. The Edge 1050 was one of a new generation of larger bike computers, but it was also relatively lightweight. It meant that not every single out-front mount had to be completely redesigned, but some did, and according to K-Edge, the weight of a bike computer actually matters a lot when you start trying to hang lights under it. The Edge 1060 is a genuine improvement here, offering a 19-gram weight reduction, dropping from 161g down to 142g. Likely more important to more people, though, the outer dimensions have also been reduced. The 1060 shrinks its overall footprint by over a centimeter in length (106.9mm down from 118.5mm) and it’s narrower by about 2mm. That will help with tight fitment on some out-front mounts—I’m looking at you, Specialized—but since Garmin is using the exact same 3.5-inch touchscreen, that physical size reduction has to mean smaller bezels.

The software experience on the Edge 1060 also sees some updates with an eye on streamlining ride preparation and on-the-road navigation. Garmin has refined the interface by adding a QWERTY keyboard, a new staging checklist, and more customizable home screen layouts, allowing riders to easily reorganize widgets and status pages. Beyond the menus, the device introduces smarter routing capabilities. It’s now possible to compare different route options based on metrics like elevation or bike type, preview upcoming road hazards and traffic before starting, or use the “Free Flow” setting to prioritize paths with the fewest stops and intersections to maintain speed during training efforts. If coffee rides are more your thing, “Up Ahead” notifications will flag approaching points of interest like cafes or restrooms.

If an $800 bike computer is not on your list of future purchases, Garmin is also updating the brand’s lower-priced options that are aimed at riders who want simpler ride tracking and routing features. The Edge Explore 3 is landing at $399.99 while the Edge Explore 3 Plus adds a built-in speaker and microphone, the same as in the Edge 1060, for an extra $100. For those who are comparing, that matches up with the Edge 550 at $499.99, but the Explore series offers a larger screen with touch functionality in exchange for performance-focused details such as smart fueling alerts, electronic groupset integration, and advanced training metrics like real-time stamina and power guide. The Explore series also offers many of the same new routing features found on the flagship 1060, including community-reported road hazard alerts, point-of-interest notifications, and the ability to drop a location pin directly from Apple or Google Maps on a smartphone to immediately generate a bike-specific route. This series is also catered to commuters with Shimano and Bosch e-bike system integrations to display current assist levels and battery life, alongside a new tracking profile that calculates the real-time carbon savings of a given ride. Battery life for the Edge Explore series is quoted as up to 14 hours of demanding use for Explore 3 Plus, while the base Explore 3 stretches that to 16 hours.

The final launch today is a look ahead to the coming winter. The Tacx Nēra is an all-new entry that drops the price of technology significantly with some trickle-down efficiencies. While it’s hardly cheap at $999.99, this is really a budget version of the $1,999.99 Tacx Neo 3M.…

items.title: 32-inch Gravel Gains Steam with New Tires from Continental and Rene Herse
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The tire offerings from both big and small brands build on the rumors that 32-inch wheel gravel bikes from big brands will be rolling out early next year.
items.lbText:
In anticipation of next year, when many brands are rumored to be launching 32-inch gravel bikes, two new tires fit for that new wheel standard have been announced. Over the past week, both Continental and Rene Herse announced they will be releasing 32-inch gravel tires in April 2027.

At Big Sugar, Continental unveiled its new 32-inch Dubnital tire that will launch in April. The tire is virtually unchanged from the 700c Dubnital and adds size optionality to the 32-inch width spectrum.

The Rene Herse Indiana Pass will also add to the same category with a 55mm semi-slick option, despite the brand’s CEO’s skepticism of the viability of the new wheel size.

While the Dubnital is the first move to big tires from Continental, this is very much the beginning of a broader push.

Considering the comments the brand has made in it’s soft launch of the 32-inch Dubnital, Continental will add to that 32-inch catalog soon, but on the initial run it will be just the 50mm version of the brand’s popular gravel and cross-country tread.

The Dubnital 32-inch will be available in the race-rapid compound and casing configuration, Continental’s fastest setup for its gravel and mountain bike tires, and is slated to be one of the few 50mm, 32-inch gravel tires.

“The growing interest in 32” wheels is clear, and our priority is ensuring riders have immediate access to Continental’s flagship tire technologies as new wheel sizes emerge,” said Alexander Haenke, Product Manager for MTB & Gravel at Continental Tires. “Choosing the Dubnital as our first 32” release allows us to support evolving setup preferences and frame designs right out of the gate.”

Continental told Velo that the reason why the Dubnital is the first 32-inch gravel tire from the brand is because of its similarity to the 32-inch mountain bike tires the German brand had been working on.

Speaking to professionals in the industry, 32-inch gravel tires are lagging behind the mountain bike tires because R&D from the big brands on 32-inch gravel began much later than 32-inch mountain bike tech. Interestingly, come next year, when many of these 32-inch bikes start to roll out, there might be more gravel options than mountain bikes.

The Dubnital 32-inch 50mm tire will be a key addition to the market because when those gravel bikes start to roll out, there are not tons of great gravel-sized tire options.

Similarly, Rene Herse has also announced 32-inch tires that will enter the 50-55mm width market to meet the anticipated demand that will come from the new bikes. The Rene Herse Indiana Pass, named after the high point of the Tour Divide, uses the Rene Herse semi-slick tread, will come in four different constructions, and will be available in 55mm.

Rene Herse is a notable entry into the 32-inch tire game because Jan Hiene, the brand’s CEO, has been a vocal opponent of the bigger wheel size. He was so vociferous in this stance that we hosted a debate between Heine and John Karrasch, one of 32-inch wheels most vocal proponents of 32-inch wheels, on the Velo podcast .

The flip from the brand doesn’t seem to be a change of opinion. Instead, it was a response to requests from Rene Herse’s professional athletes to have tires to support the new bikes they will be riding in 2027. In particular, the tires will support Meaghan Hackinen, the 2026 Tour Divide winner who will race the Salsa Fargo 32 next year, and gravel pros Ted King and Brennan Wertz.

“Both Ted and Brennan are tall and very strong riders, so they are perfect candidates to benefit from the larger wheels,” Jan Heine said in the press release. “They are curious about the new wheel size, but they don’t want to give up the speed, comfort and grip of their supple Rene Herse semi-slicks. That’s why we’ll offer their favorite tires in the 32-inch size.”

Neither of these tires are available yet, as both tires are set to roll out in April.

items.title: Jayco, Picnic Confirm WorldTour Plans for 2027 Despite Registration Hiccups
items.author: ahood
items.content: Jayco-AlUla and Picnic-PostNL explain their UCI registration delays and confirm both plan to race in the 2027 WorldTour.
items.lbText:
Officials from both Picnic-PostNL and Jayco-AlUla confirmed they are still seeking WorldTour licenses in 2027. (Photo: Getty Images)

Jayco-AlUla and Picnic-PostNL say they are preparing for the 2027 WorldTour season despite missing the UCI’s first registration deadline , officials from both teams confirmed to Velo .

So far, it’s just paperwork, with a bank guarantee delay and an unresolved equipment partnership holding up their applications.

Both organizations explained their absence from the UCI’s initial registration lists published Monday. The omissions affect their men’s and women’s WorldTour programs.

Neither has been refused registration, because both have time to complete their files before the UCI publishes its final list December 8.

Jayco’s parent organization, GreenEDGE Cycling, said the delay impacting Jayco-AlUla and Liv AlUla Jayco is due to an international banking procedure.

“We are aware that Team Jayco AlUla and Liv AlUla Jayco’s names are absent from the recent UCI teams registration list,” a press note read.

“This is purely due to a technical transfer process that will be resolved very soon. Processing the bank guarantee required by the UCI involves cross-border financial operations that sometimes can encounter delays.”

GreenEDGE said preparations for next season continue for the Aussie-backed team that’s been in the peloton since 2012. Daniel Benson has reported a new title partner is coming online, but so far, there is no official confirmation.

“We can confirm that GreenEDGE Cycling’s planning and preparation for the 2027 season remains on track and we looking forward to racing our 16th season in the WorldTour,” officials said.

Picnic-PostNL said its outstanding paperwork concerns a technical partnership following the bankruptcy of its current partner’s company.

The team recently made headlines following a report of a toxic team environment , something several staffers and riders denied.

The team did not identify the technical partner in its statement or give a date for completing the agreement.

“Our Men and Women’s programs are currently in the application process for WorldTour status in the coming year,” a statement read. “To this end, the team still needs to provide information relating to the finalization of a partnership with a technical partner for the coming season, following the bankruptcy of the current partner’s company. We will be doing this in the coming period.”

Despite a rough 2026 season , the statement confirms that Picnic-PostNL will be pursuing WorldTour status.

There were some suggestions from a source that told Velo that the team might step down to a ProTeam license in 2027, but the team’s statement Tuesday suggests it intends to remain at the WorldTour.

The explanations came after the UCI’s October 15 deadline for applicants to submit essential registration documents.

If both teams see their paperwork filed and in order, that will mean that 18 men’s and 14 women’s teams will race at the top-level WorldTour category in 2027.

Those licenses are important because it gives team automatic invitations to the team’s most important stage races and one-day classics, including the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes.

Missing the initial deadline does not prevent teams from securing registration, although it can carry consequences for rider contracts.

“In accordance with the UCI Regulations and subject to other applicable provisions, riders from these teams may terminate their contracts early, but this right will lapse if their team is subsequently registered,” the UCI stated.

Ben O’Connor is leaving Jayco-AlUla for Decathlon CMA-CGM in a move confirmed Tuesday, but that deal was signed months ago and was a result of the team’s filing delay, sources said.

There are another few tidbits in the team registry.

Modern Adventure Factor Racing appears among the men’s ProTeam applicants, confirming earlier reports that Factor would be joining the George Hincapie project for 2027 and beyond as a co-sponsor .

Soudal also loses Quick-Step as a co-title sponsor and will be called Soudal-Safety Jogger for 2027, making an end of an era for the Belgian flooring company.

Quick-Step was either title or co-sponsor of the team since its founding in 2003, and co-sponsor of Mapei from 1999 to 2002. The company will remain a partner backer of the team.

items.title: Why Does an Event Like BorderLands Gravel Matter?
items.author: Kelly Matkovich
items.content: A gravel race along the Arizona-Mexico border is introducing riders to Douglas, where history, hospitality, and the Geronimo Trail meet.
items.lbText:
The Arizona borderlands is a geographic and cultural region on the northern side of the Arizona-Mexico border. To talk about the borderlands area as a whole transcends the line on the map and is where the two countries meet.

While the topic of the border has been hotly contested in the current political environment, the history of the border shows it’s not only been complicated, but the border itself has moved. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War in 1848. As a result, the United States purchased land that is now California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Arizona and New Mexico. Five years later came the Gadsden Purchase, where the U.S. added even more land, which includes where Douglas, Arizona, sits today. While Douglas wasn’t officially incorporated until 1905, that meant if you lived in the area, you went to bed in Mexico, and the next day, you woke up, and the land was now part of the United States.

It’s complicated and yet beautiful at the same time.

This paints the backdrop for the BorderLands Gravel race , which starts and finishes in the border town of Douglas. Sure, it would’ve been easy to start writing about the race itself, focusing on the course, the mileage, podium winners, and more. However, once the racers left the pavement a short distance outside of town, the gravel road veered south, and the most prominent feature right before our eyes was the Arizona-Mexico border wall. It’s about context. Sitting just about 4,000 feet in elevation, Douglas exists in the transitional zone between the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts. Now in its third year, BorderLands Gravel returns to Douglas on November 14, 2026.

One of the questions surrounding the event for me was this: why does an event like BorderLands Gravel matter? Along with that, other questions pop up. What impact does a gravel race in Douglas have? What value or benefit does it bring to the community? Also, why did racers travel, in some cases, great distances to ride and race this stretch of desert gravel roads along the border?

As to why this matters for the community of Douglas, we need to first look at some data.

According to the “2024 Outdoor Participation Trend Report” by the Outdoor Foundation and the Outdoor Industry Association, “In 2023, the outdoor recreation participant base grew 4.1% to a record 175.8 million participants: 57.3% of all Americans aged six and older” (p. 3). Americans continue to get outside to recreate. Even more so, of the 175.8 million participants in outdoor recreation, 17.2% of them recreated on a bicycle. That number equates to 30+ million Americans enjoying the outdoors by bike.

At the same time, as more people recreate outdoors, it is having a positive economic impact. Outdoor adventuring consumers spend $887 billion annually. That results in 7.6 million jobs, $65.3 billion in federal tax revenue, and $59.2 billion in state and local tax revenue. In Arizona, consumers spend $21.2 billion on outdoor recreation, which funds 201,000 jobs, $5.7 billion in wages and salaries, and $1.4 billion in state and local tax revenue.

Lastly, as it pertains specifically to gravel cycling, it has been experiencing an explosion of growth. Not only are innumerable bike brands creating whole lines of gravel-specific bicycles, but races and events like BorderLands Gravel are on the rise. According to BikeReg’s 2025 year-end data , gravel race registrations have grown more than tenfold since 2015, far outpacing mountain bike, road, cyclocross, and recreational events. Simply put, more people are enjoying the outdoors on gravel bikes.

For communities across Arizona, there’s an impetus to strategically and thoughtfully tap into the resource of capturing spending on outdoor recreation. That’s why events like BorderLands Gravel matter for a community like Douglas.

While Douglas has a stable employment base due to its shared border with Agua Prieta, one of the challenges is its rural location. However, where some see challenges or even weaknesses, others see opportunities. Suppose you’re going to host a gravel cycling race. In that case, you need some basic agreements that Douglas has in abundance … miles of gravel roads, stunning desert scenery, mild temperatures, the City of Douglas staff on board, and innumerable stakeholders, agencies, and landowners linking arms to make the race happen. In other words, the whole community was on board and behind it. Even more so, you need a visionary spearheading the event and tethering together all of these pieces and relationships. That’s why race organizer Mike Miller is the straw that stirs this drink.

However, it’s more than the economic impact; it’s about showcasing the community of Douglas and the beautiful surrounding landscape.

As Mike Miller dreamed of this event, Douglas became the unexpected destination for a premier gravel cycling event, thanks to the storied Gadsden Hotel. Inspired by the hotel’s historic charm, the vision for a gravel bike race on the iconic Geronimo Trail began to take shape. The process kicked off in November 2023, with a meeting between Mike and the Gadsden Hotel’s General Manager, followed by discussions with local tourism and city officials. By January 2024, the concept had gained official backing, setting the stage for an event that would showcase Douglas’s rich heritage and rugged terrain.…

items.title: My Death Valley Heat Training Failed Miserably. Here Is What I Learned.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: If you are prepping for a huge ride in the desert, consistency beats intensity. Learn exactly what heat training is, how to do it outside, and why my approach completely backfired.
items.lbText:
In 2024, I rode 1,000km from Reno to Las Vegas, with the big draw being a chance to cruise through Death Valley. What sounded great on paper turned into 30 mph headwinds and temperatures up to 110°F (43°C). On the 3,000-foot climb out of the valley, I could only manage about 500 feet of elevation at a time before collapsing under a scrubby bush for 10 minutes to rest and regroup. Needless to say, I was looking for redemption.

I wanted another crack at the desert adventure, but I certainly didn’t want to relive that heat horror, so I decided to try heat training. It’s essentially repeated exposure to enough heat stress to force your body to adapt. For more scientific insight, I reached out to Brian Maiorano, Coach Liaison at CORE Body Temperature, to find out what’s actually happening inside your body during the process.

“When you consistently cause the body stress by raising your heat strain index, it says, hey, I don’t like this. This is causing me more work,” Maiorano explained. “Your body then adapts by creating more blood plasma. And that extra blood plasma is what allows you to start sweating earlier and start sweating more profusely.”

It’s that increased plasma volume that gives you a more effective sweat response, helping your body better manage the physiological stress of exercising in the heat. Sounds ideal. So how do you actually do it?

I don’t own a bike trainer. I’m the type of cyclist who would ride through a hurricane before I sit on a hamster wheel. (Spoiler alert: we did hit the tail end of a hurricane in the desert, but more on that later). So when it came to heat training, my only option was outside. My inspiration was that now-iconic social media video of Tom Pidcock heat training for Worlds , so I basically recreated it. I wore a full wool winter kit, topped with a CORE Body Temperature Tyvek suit. Over that, I added a Rapha down jacket with the hood up, plus thick restaurant freezer gloves—the kind you saw Jonas Vingegaard using at the fish factory. I added sweat shorts over the Tyvek suit to help block the wind, winter shoe covers, a wool cap, my puffy hood, and finally my helmet.

It was giving Beastie Boys in the “Intergalactic” music video. I looked absolutely deranged. I was also hot, and that was the goal. I used this setup to bike outside three times a week for three weeks, and each session lasted one to two hours.

According to Maiorano, the strategy I had in mind was possible. “You can do it on a road bike,” he says, but the focus needs to be getting “your layering more dialed in to prevent the wind evaporation.” In other words, the challenge isn’t necessarily creating enough heat; it’s keeping your body from getting rid of it. On a road bike, the constant airflow helps sweat evaporate and cool you, which is exactly what you’re trying to limit. Maiorano explains, “Try a normal cycling kit, but then over top of that, a snug rain jacket and snug rain pants. And then thermal layers on top of the rain jacket. The reason you don’t want the thermal layers underneath is because you’re the one generating the sweat. If you get the thermal layers wet trapped inside the rain jacket, they’ll get soaked and cool you off. So thermal layers on the outside.” You’ll notice, this was my first of many mistakes.

A CORE sensor will certainly do the trick but I started my training block without one. The sensor tracks a metric called a heat strain index, which combines your core temperature and your skin temperature. “The heat strain index goes from 0 to 10,” Maiorano explains. “For heat training, that magic spot is 3 to 7. You just want to get in there and hold that for 45 minutes, 60 minutes, 90 minutes if you’re really looking for an intense session.”

If you don’t have a sensor, Maiorano says he used to tell his athletes to “go cook yourself, but don’t overcook yourself.” The obvious problem: What exactly does that even mean? A sensor gives athletes a target, but over time it can also teach you what an appropriate heat session feels like. Maiorano compares it to riding with a power meter: eventually, you can probably guess your power within a few watts without looking down. Heat training can work the same way.

The honest answer? Not great. My husband Richard was following the same heat-training protocol as I was. In fact, he even had hotter weather to train in during an elusive San Francisco summer heat wave while I was travelling. But on day one of our three-day trip, 109 miles into a 160-mile day, he was puking in the bushes with temperatures hitting 109°F. Day two is where the wheels fell off for me.

I was riding in the remnants of Hurricane Rachel, battling a diabolical headwind through Death Valley that had me, Josh Ross, Mike Levy, and other friends doing everything we could to hold 10 mph in a full echelon across the road. After three hours of unrelenting wind, my speed had dropped to 8 mph and I was done. I sat under that well-known Death Valley scrubby bush and tried to regroup. After what felt like an eternity—which was probably only 10 minutes—I got back on my bike and was immediately dizzy, with zero power in my legs. Game over.

Sadly, I didn’t even make it to the 3,000-foot climb out of the valley, which I had originally thought would be the true heat-training test. Instead, I got to test whether my iPhone satellite feature would work to get an SOS text to our friends running SAG. Desert: 1. Lisa: 0.

Was it the heat that actually did me in? According to Maiorano, on an ultra-endurance ride, it’s not that simple. Heat, fatigue, and fueling can compound on each other. Overheating increases cardiovascular strain and can interfere with digestion and fueling, while inadequate fueling can further compromise performance.…

items.title: These 5 Transfers Will Transform Pro Cycling in 2027
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Broken contracts and big promises: All the stakes and key narratives behind the 5 transfers that will reshape the men's peloton next year.
items.lbText:
Grand tour winners, former world champions, and one of USA’s hottest talents will make career-defining transfers this winter.

Richard Carapaz, Giulio Ciccone, Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Andrew “AJ” August are the headline names making moves in a wildly busy transfer window that’s already seen Tom Pidcock get a superteam and Lidl-Trek go transfer crazy.

These five blockbuster moves promise the riders more freedom, leadership opportunities, and career progression. They offer the teams victories from Paris-Roubaix through the Tour de France.

Broken contracts, bizarre motivations, and troubled teams accompany some of these biggest moves of 2026-2027.

Here’s all you need to know about the five biggest transfers in the men’s peloton, as of October 20.

Stay tuned for a similar feature on some whopper contracts in the women’s sport.

For Carapaz: How does Richard Carapaz benefit by moving to NSN Cycling Team?

If you’ve got an answer, please let us know.

This feels like a sideways, or maybe even a backward move for one of the top-ranked riders in the world.

EF Education-EasyPost isn’t the best GC team in the world, but it’s been good enough to put Carapaz into the top-4 of a grand tour for three years in a row. Plus, it allowed its biggest rider the flexibility to roam free. Stage hunting, the KoM classification, GC – nothing was off-limits for Carapaz at EF.

What does NSN have to offer Carapaz (beyond a bigger paycheck)?

The Swiss-registered squad was a sprint-focused team in its debut 2026 season.

It’s bolstered its climbing division with Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt for 2027, but is still short on the climbing support Carapaz might need if he wants to go big at the Tour de France.

Beyond that, Carapaz might not get such a long leash at an ambitious team that clearly wants to break into GC racing. Here’s hoping he can keep bringing the panache.

For NSN Cycling Team: The answer is obvious – the team gets possibly the most exciting racer in the world. Carapaz will bring the team results, charisma, and guaranteed TV time.

Luring Carapaz from EF was the heist of the season , and by far the biggest transfer in the men’s peloton so far.

Carapaz broke his contract with EF to join NSN.

There’s no rumor of bad blood between the Ecuadorian superstar and the American team that gave him free rein over his racing ambitions. It just supported him through one of the best seasons of his career.

EF boss Jonathan Vaughters confirmed this week to Escape Collective that he’s suffering a budget crunch – something already evident in the exodus of talent leaving the team this winter and its sparse recruitment policy.

Maybe NSN made Carapaz an offer he couldn’t refuse, and one that Vaughters couldn’t match. The likelihood of a buyout fee would have made it a reluctant no-brainer for the impoverished American team.

For Ciccone: Giulio Ciccone will be a great white shark at Pinarello-Q36.5, having been one of many fish in an overflowing pond at Lidl-Trek.

The exuberant Italian will join Tom Pidcock as one of the ultimate bigs at Pinarello-Q36.5, which is rapidly emerging as one of the most audacious, ambitious teams in the bunch.

How Ciccone and Pidcock divide the calendar and their ambitions is another matter. Scheduling two top riders with such similar skill sets won’t be simple.

For Pinarello-Q36.5: Ciccone could have won GP Québec, the European championships, and Il Lombardia in the last month. When combined with Pidcock and Mauro Schmid, Pinarello-Q36.5 will have the ultimate triple-threat on suitably punchy parcours.

And if Pinarello-Q36.5 has Ciccone, Pidcock, and Schmid divide and conquer, they’ll be drowning in the UCI points they need to hit the WorldTour in 2029.

Ciccone was signed with Lidl-Trek through 2029. However, the 31-year-old was reportedly rubbed the wrong way by the recent management overhaul and identity shift at his long-time team. The Italian was a close ally of former team boss Luca Guercilena, who appears to have been squeezed out of his role in the team’s structural upheaval.

The overload of GC racers at Lidl-Trek no doubt improved Cicco’s mood, either.

This seems to have been an ugly divorce. The statements from Ciccone and Lidl-Trek confirming their contract termination couldn’t have been frostier.

For Ganna: Filippo Ganna needed a reboot, bad. The towering Italian has huge potential, and it’s been going untapped.

Sure, Remco Evenepoel is unbeatable against the clock right now, but Ganna’s proven he can be a lot more than just a time trialist. Remember his forays into bunch sprinting? Or his barnstorming breakaway antics at the 2020 Giro?

Aside from his spectacular win at Dwars Door Vlaanderen, Ganna lost his road-racing chops this season.

Ganna must see a move to Lidl-Trek as a new chapter.

New management, new motivation, and a team committed to classics racing and sprinting might restore the true “Top Ganna.”

For Lidl-Trek: Lidl-Trek must have watched the Italian track pursuit team and liked what it saw. Just imagine Ganna leading out his Italian pursuit teammate Jonathan Milan at the Giro d’Italia?! Bellissimo .

Ganna will bring Lidl-Trek a leadout man de-luxe and a heavyweight addition to its already hulking classics squad next year.

Ganna, Milan, Mads Pedersen, and Mathias Vacek could flatten even the most gnarled, off-set cobblestones of Paris-Roubaix. In a race as unpredictable as “The Hell of the North,” this type of full-frontal offense could compensate for Lidl-Trek not having a Pogi, Wout, or Mathieu.

Sadly for Lidl-Trek, multiple second-tier leaders aren’t so advantageous in grand tours, as we’re about to explore …

Ganna split from Netcompany Ineos a year early, and it seems like the British team did little to stop it from happening. According to Domestique , Netcompany Ineos didn’t demand a transfer payment from Lidl-Trek and may have even sweetened the deal.…

items.title: Specialized and Quick-Step End One of the Most Important Partnerships in Pro Cycling
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Wildly successful 18-year era comes to a close: US brand shifts focus to ongoing partnerships and Belgian team moves on with Merida.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images))

Specialized bikes and team Quick-Step officially ended one of the most significant partnerships in road racing Monday.

Both the U.S. bike behemoth and the long-running Belgian team confirmed Monday the end of an 18-year collaboration that brought the so-called “Wolf Pack” more than 800 victories.

Beginning in 2007, the partnership put the Specialized logo on top of the biggest races in the world and helped develop some of the most popular road bikes on the market.

The split marks the end of an era in professional cycling.

The collaboration between the brand and the team was one of the longest, most successful partnerships in the peloton.

Quick-Step riders won cobblestone monuments, Tour de France stages, and world titles on various iterations of the Tarmac, Shiv, and Venge. Riders like Tom Boonen, Mark Cavendish, and Remco Evenepoel are among the superstars who forged their palmarés on the brand’s bikes.

In return, the team helped Specialized refine some of its most successful models sold to the mass market .

Cavendish and Evenepoel are known to have been particularly active in developing its sprint and TT bikes, respectively.

The collaboration began in 2007, paused in 2010 and 2011, and has continued since 2012.

The news that the end was nigh was first reported , though not confirmed, in April.

Separate social media posts by both Specialized and Soudal Quick-Step on Monday made it official.

“After nearly two decades together, we’ve celebrated some of the sport’s most iconic moments, including victories in monument classics, grand tours, world championships, and countless stage races,” Specialized wrote on an Instagram post Monday.

“Thank you to the riders, staff, management, and fans who helped make this partnership so memorable and wishes Soudal Quick-Step and AG Insurance-Soudal continued success in the years ahead.”

It will be all change for the team currently known as Soudal Quick-Step in 2027.

The team will ride Merida Bikes and be known as Soudal Safety Jogger.

The Belgian flooring company Quick-Step steps down from its title sponsorship of the team for the first time in 24 years this winter.

Meanwhile, Merida will return to the peloton after it was last seen in 2025 with Bahrain Victorious. The Taiwanese manufacturer owns a 35 percent stake in Specialized.

The partnering women’s team AG Insurance-Soudal will also switch from Specialized to Merida in 2027.

With the Quick-Step team off the books, Specialized will tighten its focus on its ongoing partnerships.

The California-based brand will continue to invest in its partnerships with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, FDJ United-Suez United, SD Worx Protime, and the Specialized Factory Racing off-road superteam .

Demi Vollering, Remco Evenepoel, Keegan Swenson, and Lotte Kopecky will be its biggest-name athletes going forward.

MTB star Kate Courtney will also ride Specialized on the road after she made her bombshell move to FDJ United Suez this summer.

Tim Merlier won Quick-Step’s last race on a Specialized bike Sunday at the Eneco Tour. The Belgian super-sprinter gave his bike an affectionate tap after he blasted across the finishline.

“I think it is my 80th professional victory. I don’t know how many I have achieved on a Specialized [57 – ed], but since I started riding this brand of bikes, I’ve achieved many victories,” Merlier said at the finish Sunday.

“I’m very proud that I can finish this season with a victory for Specialized,” he said.

It was a suitably winning end to one of the winningest, most recognizable partnerships in pro road racing.

items.title: Daria Pikulik Keeps Olympic Silver Despite 18-Month Whereabouts Ban
items.author: ahood
items.content: Polish cyclist Daria Pikulik hasn't raced since March after 18-month ban, but she keeps her Paris Olympic medal.
items.lbText:
Daria Pikulik, right, was hit with an 18-month whereabouts ban. (Photo: Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

Olympic silver medalist Daria Pikulik has been hit with an 18-month whereabouts ban, but will keep her Olympic medal, the International Testing Agency announced Monday.

The Polish rider’s ban ran from December 9, 2024, through June 8, 2026. All results and prizes during that period are disqualified, but there were no major victories.

Her Paris Olympic silver remains on her palmarès because she won it before the sanction period.

Pikulik finished behind American Jennifer Valente and ahead of New Zealand’s Ally Wollaston in the August 2024 omnium in Paris.

“It was never my intention to violate anti-doping rules,” Pikulik wrote in a statement on Instagram, translated from Polish.

The ITA, which runs the UCI’s independent anti-doping program, said Pikulik committed three whereabouts failures within 12 months.

Pikulik, 29, said the missed tests occurred in September and October 2023, followed by a third in September 2024.

“I spent the past two years trying to defend my good name,” she wrote.

Pikulik said the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled against her in March 2026 without determining a sanction. She said the suspension was finalized in September.

The road and track rider, who raced for Human Powered Health, also addressed her absence from competition since March.

“This was an incredibly difficult time for me and those closest to me,” she wrote. “Throughout my career, I have undergone dozens of doping tests without any problems.

“However, I must accept what happened and put it behind me,” Pikulik wrote. “I apologize to everyone I have let down, and I thank everyone who stood by me during this time.”
